issues.title: Add custom comment to excluded "unsafe" package
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Pip-compile users may consider a package to be "unsafe" to pin for a variety of reasons: e.g. necessary security patches, bloated dependency chains, multiple providers of the same python package, etc. Currently, there is no option to customize the `requirements.txt` comment indicating a package is unsafe. They all have the same header:
```
# The following packages are considered to be unsafe in a requirements file:
# opencv-python
```
From just this information, it's unclear *why* `opencv-python` is unsafe. Is there a security vulnerability? Or is a different reason as listed above?

#### Describe the solution you'd like
Ideally, each package can explain why it was excluded. As one example:

```bash
pip-compile --no-allow-unsafe \
    --unsafe-package "opencv-python  # has many providers such as  opencv-python-headless, opencv-contrib-python, etc. so no need to force a more bloated option" \
    --unsafe-package "another-package  # with it's reason for exclusion"
```

#### Alternative solutions
It would also make sense if an `--exclude` option was present instead, which generates the heading:

```
# The following packages are listed as dependencies, but explicitly excluded from this requirements file:
# package-a
```

Or something similar. I am filing this request under `allow-unsafe` instead of an additional `--exclude` flag since https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/333 is marked as closed with the suggestion people use this instead.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body: The solution is to list your direct deps in a `.in` file instead of the command-line. The command-line args don't usually get complicated processing, but the input files would have that. The resulting constraints `.txt` probably shouldn't contain these comments anyway. The input file is the right place for those comments.

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
Overall our CI status is much better than it used to be, but it's still flaky. And it's easy for someone to contribute a flaky test without anyone realizing that it's flaky.

I see two main issues at present, which are related:

- Relying on the network (actual package installation, notably `setuptools`)
- Unstable run times, which sometimes unexpectedly spends our full time limit and makes jobs fail (notable on Windows pypy, which seems to be our worst performer anecdotally)

---

The one major improvement I have in mind for us is to use in-tree build backends for our testing. I need to allocate time to work on this, but I want single-file backends with the following behaviors:

- `fails-if-invoked-backend`: implements PEP 517 hooks and raises errors whenever they are called (testing failure modes, testing that static metadata reads are really static)
  👍 I'm confident this is useful.
- `dynamic-only-backend`: implements PEP 517 hooks and only supports dynamic fields for everything other than `name`, where all fields are actually pulled from some easy source for tests to write (maybe a `tool` table), good for testing dynamic metadata behaviors
  👍 I'm confident this is useful.
- `static-only-backend`: implements PEP 517 hooks but only supports static fields; absolutely nothing is dynamic -- useful for trees of fake packages, where real builds of wheels may be invoked (you could do this with `dynamic-only`, but I think the pair makes sense)
  🤔 I think this is useful?
- `wrapper-backend`: a backend which requires a `tool` config to tell it which backend to actually run, provides hooks which literally just call some other backend's hooks -- good for testing of second-order build deps
  🤷 This makes sense, but I'm not really sure it's useful?

I have another project where I'd like these backends as well. They might be useful for other packaging projects.

issues.title: Implement PEP 751 "A file format to list Python dependencies for installation reproducibility" (a.k.a. lock files | `pylock.toml` | `pylock.*.toml`)
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Proper ecosystem-standard lock files are getting traction yet again and we have to keep up. This will allow us to work with more ecosystem tooling than just pip, uniformly covering more use cases. And personally, I'm just thrilled to see this PEP implemented across the Python Packaging ecosystem.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

Implementation of whatever's possible, including both lock file types. The feature should be marked as experimental until [PEP 751](https://peps.python.org/pep-0751/) is marked as accepted. But it should give people opportunity to try it out and perhaps feed the feedback back into the upstream discussion.

#### Alternative Solutions

Not doing anything..?

#### Additional context

This is a follow-up for #1526 that @brettcannon opened years ago.

The initial discussion is @ https://discuss.python.org/t/lock-files-again-but-this-time-w-sdists/46593.

The current open discussion is @ https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-751-lock-files-again/59173.

> As this widens the goals of `requirements.txt`

`pip-compile`'s output is more of a `constraints.txt` situation. Given a `pip-compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt`, one would be able to `pip install -r requirements.in -c requirements.txt`.

> I think makes sense to make it a new-subcommand to allow full flexibility of an interface that makes sense for the widened scope.

For multi-target resolutions, maybe. But I'd rather start with something that can output the same `constraints.txt` as TOML (through a CLI option for different format) in `pip-compile` paired with the support of `pip-sync` for installing from pylock.

---

FTR, this issue was never about resolving the tree for foreign platforms. In fact, it's been seen questionable for a long time: #826. I'd rather have multiple pylock files with the platform encoded in their names to match the current practice, initially. Merging multiple non-matching resolutions is a separate discussion and embedding it into this effort may end up delaying the progress indefinitely.

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
I support the path in #2380 in which there is a _new_ `pip-lock` command. We're changing the output format, and that has some associated semantics. I don't think it makes sense to try to bundle that with the existing `pip-compile` command. I have been operating, up until now, on the assumption that we'd make this part of `pip-compile`, but coming in with a new command gives us a lot more freedom.

I would like to treat this as a relatively rare opportunity to re-examine some of our CLI to decide how things fit together.
(e.g., I saw that currently `pip-lock` carries over a lot of the `pip-compile` options. Maybe we should start with fewer? But I would have to look through them all to see which ones I might suggest cutting.)

Relatedly, I think we can label the command as "experimental" in its initial releases, giving ourselves, officially, permission to tweak the CLI experience around it as needed until we have some time to see what issues come in.

The solution in #2380 for doing matrix-style resolution on multiple platforms is to walk different user-selected markers and rerun resolution, patching part of `packaging` to provide the desired markers to `pip`'s resolver. The requirement to patch is the one place where I get a bit uncertain. I'd like to at least share what we're looking at with the `pip` maintainers and see if they have significant concerns -- beyond the standing issue that we're using non-public APIs and own the burdens associated with that.

In my experience, requiring multiple locks, rather than having a unified lockfile capability, is something which significantly reduces the number of projects in which I use `pip-tools`. If we can get that capability here, I think it would be a very significant win for the new command.

---

As a bit of process/review note, particularly for @gaborbernat to be aware:
I've had very limited FOSS time lately, but we need to get out a release which fixes `pip-sync` compatibility with 26.1 . Even if `pip-lock` is ready soon, I don't plan to try to review+include it in our next release.

comments.author: gaborbernat
comments.body:
Thanks Stephen and Sviatoslav for the careful reads. Replying to both in one comment.

## On the new-command path

Stephen, agreed that a separate `pip-lock` is the right shape. PEP 751 is structurally different enough from `requirements.txt` that the two should not share an entry point, and a fresh command lets the surface settle on its own contract.

Sviatoslav, on widening `requirements.txt`: the pylock side does not extend that informal format. PEP 751 is a published spec with its own data model (structured `dependencies` per package, hashes mandatory, markers as the unified-environment mechanism), and `pip-lock`'s job is to be spec-conformant rather than to grow `requirements.txt`. The two outputs coexist; nothing in this PR touches `pip-compile`'s contract.

## On the CLI surface

Stephen, to your point about starting with fewer flags: most of the trim against `pip-compile` is already done. `pip-lock` drops 12 flags whose only purpose was the `requirements.txt` text format:

| Dropped from `pip-compile` | Why pylock.toml does not need it |
| --- | --- |
| `--annotate`, `--annotation-style` | each package carries a structured `dependencies` array; annotations are part of the data model |
| `--emit-find-links`, `--emit-index-url`, `--emit-options`, `--emit-trusted-host` | each package carries `index = "..."`; tool metadata lives in `[tool.pip-tools]` |
| `--generate-hashes`, `--reuse-hashes` | hashes are mandatory in PEP 751; the field is not optional |
| `--header` | replaced by `created-by` and the `[tool.pip-tools]` provenance block |
| `--newline` | text-format trivia |
| `--resolver` | the legacy resolver is gone |
| `--strip-extras` | extras are encoded structurally as markers, not stripped post-hoc |

The 9 added flags map to specific PEP 751 / PEP 735 capabilities the new format requires:

| Added in `pip-lock` | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--check` | re-resolves in memory, exits non-zero on drift; the CI hook for "is the lock up to date?" without writing |
| `-j/--jobs` | caps the worker-process pool that resolves cohorts in parallel; defaults to `auto` (one per CPU, capped at cohort count) |
| `--platform` | adds a target platform (`linux-x86_64`, `windows-amd64`, …) to the lock matrix |
| `--python-version` | adds a target Python `MAJOR.MINOR` (or `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) to the lock matrix |
| `--no-universal` | restricts to the host's platform and Python only; the host-only escape hatch |
| `--group` | includes a PEP 735 `[dependency-groups]` group in resolution |
| `--all-groups` | includes every declared PEP 735 group |
| `--no-metadata` / `--no-tool-block` | suppresses the `[tool.pip-tools]` block, for projects that want a frozen byte-stable lock independent of pip-tools provenance |
| `--skip-metadata-field` | omits a specific volatile field (e.g. `generated-at`, `pip-version`) so CI diffs do not churn |

The remaining 33 shared with `pip-compile` are the index / auth / upgrade / cache / build-isolation surface users already know. Cutting any of those forces users into `--pip-args` for routine flows (alternate index, client cert, trusted host), so I would rather act on a specific list of flags you think are wrong than do a blanket trim. Each addition was deliberate, and each is one line to remove once there is a concrete case.

## On the marker patching

Stephen, on the patching uncertainty: `pip-lock` rewrites `packaging.markers._evaluate_markers` (in both the top-level package and pip's vendored copy) so platform comparisons evaluate to `True` for one discovery resolution. That single scan walks every platform-conditional dependency, which is what makes the cohort partitioner work. Mitigations already in the diff:

1. **First-use shape verification.** `_verify_packaging_marker_shape()` probes the AST with a known-good marker the first time it runs and raises `PipToolsError` if the shape no longer matches. Callers fall back to per-env resolution rather than emit wrong cohorts.
2. **Stable intercept point.** The patch targets `_evaluate_markers(markers, environment)` rather than `_eval_op`, because `_eval_op`'s signature shifted between pip 25.2 and 26.0, while `_evaluate_markers` and the marker-tuple shape have been stable since pip 22.2.
3. **Bounded scope.** Only platform comparisons (`sys_platform`, `platform_machine`, `platform_system`, `platform_release`, `os_name`, `platform_version`) are forced to `True`. Python-version comparisons stay honored, so the partitioner can still distinguish python-conditional cohorts.

I am comfortable shipping with this as a known non-public-API dependency that pip-tools owns the burden for, with the verification gate as the safety net. In parallel, opening a discussion with pip and packaging maintainers about a public intercept point (or an alternative API for "evaluate this marker under a relaxed environment") makes sense. Will draft that separately so this PR does not block on it.

## On the experimental labeling

Stephen, yes, landing in the next iteration:

- `pip-lock --help` opens with `pip-lock is experimental; the CLI surface and the [tool.pip-tools] block may change between releases`.
- A runtime warning fires on every invocation, suppressible via an env var.
- `[tool.pip-tools].experimental = true` lands in the lockfile so a future stable release can detect old locks.
- The README admonition prepends to the `Example usage for pip-lock` section.

Same pattern pip 26.1 uses for its own `pip lock`.

## On unified vs per-platform lockfiles

Sviatoslav, this is the part I most want to push back on. The unified-lock-with-markers shape is the largest reason most users I have talked to want PEP 751 at all. Replacing it with one file per platform would be a hard regression for those workflows: a publisher who wants downstream consumers to install the right variant from one artifact, a monorepo whose deploy pipeline picks `--group cpu` vs `--group gpu` from one canonical lock, a Dockerfile whose build stage and runtime stage read the same file and pick a `--group` at install time. All of those need one lock file that several environments can resolve against.

The merge is not divisive in practice. PEP 751 was designed with `marker = "..."` per-package precisely so several environments can live in one file unambiguously. The disjointness validator on the producer side proves no two same-name entries can both fire on a single install, and the marker evaluator on the consumer side picks one variant deterministically. uv has shipped this exact shape (`uv lock` plus `uv export --format pylock.toml`) for over a year against real-world projects, and the approach has held up.

`#826` is a different problem. That issue was about merging post-hoc `requirements.txt` files generated independently, where the input contracts differ between runs. PEP 751's universal lock solves the same surface concern at *resolve* time with a marker-aware resolver, not as a textual merge after the fact, so the failure modes `#826` flagged do not carry over.

`--no-universal` is already on the surface for users who want host-only locking, and a future flag could write `pylock.<platform>.toml` per platform if a project genuinely wants per-platform files. Making per-platform-only the *only* mode would close off the largest reason to adopt PEP 751, and I do not think pip-tools should ship that constraint.

## On release timing

Stephen, no objection at all. Happy to keep the branch green and rebasable while the pip-sync 26.1 fix ships. Not asking for inclusion in the next release.

Glad we are converging; this PR is much better for the input. 🙏

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
@sirosen @gaborbernat let my expand my previous message.

1) For the initial implementation, I was viewing  `pylock.toml` as a yet another output format. And would like the ability to just have the `constraints.txt` converted (both when writing to file or stdout). pip doesn't yet support using TOML as constraints, but it's being discussed: https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/13961. I see this as the first step towards something more complex. It's something that would be much easier to agree on compared to a new complex subcommand.
2) I'm not against a new `pip-lock` command (similar to the upstream `pip lock` subcommand and even more) but it should be implemented in stages and there's much to discuss. This is why, I wouldn't expect it to be the first stage in the context of this tracking issue I filed.
3) Again, I understand that `requirements.txt` is informal and was making the same point. But the important case is producing something that can be used as constraints semantically. I'd appreciate a PR that just adds a format converter in all the places that can output constraints; I think that `pip-sync` should also be able to produce a venv matching a `pylock.toml` file (`pip install -r pylock.toml` is already available upstream). The follow-up `pip-lock` work can then build on top of these components, and we can discuss what UX of the CLI should be.
4) We should start with a resolution that targets the current env. Universal resolution should be a follow-up because it relies on volatile properties/assumptions sometimes (which is a known problem ever since Poetry started using this approach) — I certainly wouldn't want this to be a default due to the controversy in how it may break things. If we want fast merges of PRs, this should be done in stages as I suggest (maybe with more standalone/atomic substages where possible). Currently, I can't agree with your assessment of #826 as somebody who's started it and changed his mind in the process of practicing the approach. It was not about post-generation merging at the point and still isn't. It's about having entirely different resolutions. But again, this is something that will be blocking the effort if we decide to make it a part of a PR that could otherwise get agreed on and merged sooner as a substage.

P.S. I wouldn't look at `uv` as the source of APIs, this project is primarily pip-based, after all. If `uv` has something to offer, that can be discussed, but I wouldn't default to its ideas having precedence just because it happens to be popular at a given moment in time.


---

TL;DR — implementing just an output format that supports the existing workflows is what I was seeking to get when I filed this issue originally. That's the scope. Implementing a feature with a custom resolution method and a subcommand is out of scope in #2124, but is welcome in the scope of #826.

comments.author: gaborbernat
comments.body:
I don't know what to say here. For me, for this to be something I can use, I need the full implementation. I need the full implementation to start using it. Otherwise, it offers no tangible benefits for me to adopt it today. In a hypothetical world where we would do this in stages, migrating between stages is so much effort that I would just not bother, and I would say probably a lot of other people would feel the same. 

So while I sympathize with the sentiment of trying to break it down into sub-stages for ease of review, the effort required to split it down into that and the friction that is introduced in part of the adoption makes it a deal breaker for me. 

Therefore, I would prefer for us to find a way to ship the full implementation from day one rather than try to break it down and drip feed it into sub-stages. 

Sirosen already identified some parts that are not fully related to this feature and were not too complicated to extract those to their own separate PRs and rebasing once these land, though still plenty of manual work, but breaking it into the stages is the line which I feel like I'm not comfortable with going ahead.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
FWIW, I'm not against having several PRs in a row that would all end up in the same target release bundled together. I understand that it's difficult to structure the changes in a digestible form, but that's just engineering. It's too easy to generate terrifying amounts of text these days that is not easy to trust or maintain. At least, it's not https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/30412.

I've offered you a bunch of steps, but a lot of those are actually not hard to implement, which I think helps reduce pressure on all parties. I was thinking of it as a more or less clear path towards your goal.

issues.title: Poor interaction between isolated mode and `--python-executable`
issues.body:
Running `pip-sync` with `--python-executable`, I was baffled as to why it was attempting to remove items from the local directory (any environment) and the user site directory (python-build-standalone environments with no virtual env present).

I eventually realised it was due to the following problem: even though `pip-sync` was being executed from a Python runtime configured to use isolated mode (no implied sys.path[0], no user site directory), the same was not true when `pip-sync` invoked the given Python executable to check the value of `sys.path`.

This means actually performing the sync in an isolated environment requires setting the relevant Python environment variables rather relying than solely on the `-I` command line flag:

```
PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1
PYTHONSAFEPATH=1
```

issues.title: Allow `pip-sync` to remove `pip-tools` when `--python-executable` is specified
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

I'd like to be able to remove `pip-tools` and the other protected packages when running `pip-sync --python-executable 'path/to/other/env`.

The protection makes sense when `pip-sync` is running in the Python environment being modified, but doesn't seem necessary when manipulating a separate target environment.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

`pip-sync --python-executable 'path/to/other/env` should allow removing `pip-tools` and the other protected packages from the target environment. I'd be ok with having to pass an extra option to say "no, seriously, I mean it, remove *everything* that isn't listed in the requirements files", but would prefer it if that wasn't necessary.

This came up due to the fact that `pip-compile` doesn't currently allow resolving for an environment other than the one running `pip-compile` (adding a `--python-executable` option to `pip-compile` is a much harder problem, but would technically eliminate my use case for this hopefully simpler proposal).

To work around this, I'd like to be able to temporarily install `pip-tools`, and then remove it later with `pip-sync`.

#### Alternative Solutions

Rather than running `pip-sync` directly, instead run `python -Ic "import piptools.scripts.sync, piptools.sync; piptools.sync.PACKAGES_TO_IGNORE.clear(); piptools.scripts.sync.cli()"` (with the same CLI arguments as would be passed to a direct invocation of `pip-sync`)


Edit: just noting #2117 as a trap to watch out for when using `--python-executable` with standalone Python environments.

issues.title: Config file discovery doesn't work as intended
issues.body:
As it stated in the [documentation](https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools#configuration), pip-tools look for the configuration file “in the same directory as your requirements input files”. However, due to the way click works, it's not true:

1. `--config` (and `--no-config`) is declared as eager: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/scripts/options.py#L317-L333
2. `--config`'s callback `override_defaults_from_config_file` tries to get the `src_files` param value to compute the config path relative to the source files: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/utils.py#L543
3. But since callbacks of eager options are called before other options are processed, `src_files` is always empty. From the [click documentation](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/8.1.x/advanced/#callback-evaluation-order): “All eager parameters are evaluated before all non-eager parameters, but again in the order as they were provided on the command line by the user.” 
4. `select_config_file` falls back to the current working dir as a config file location: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/utils.py#L627-L630

#### Environment Versions

1. Linux
1. Python version: `Python 3.12.3`
1. pip version: `pip 24.0`
1. pip-tools version: `pip-compile, version 7.4.1`

#### Steps to replicate

1. Create the requirements directory `requirements/` with `requirements.in`.
1. Create the configuration file `.pip-tools.toml` or `pyproject.toml` with `generate-hashes = true`.
1. Run `pip compile requirements/requirements.in`. 

#### Expected result

 `requirements/requirements.txt` contains hashes.

#### Actual result

 `requirements/requirements.txt` has no hashes; the configuration file is ignored.

I proposed it in #2048 some time ago, unfortunately it seems to have been forgotten. Thanks for providing the tests though, I might transfer them there.

issues.title: pip-compile slow and wasteful caching behavior for large packages (eg pytorch)
issues.body:
#### Environment Versions

1. Windows 10
1. Tested with Python 3.10.10 and Python 3.11.7
1. Pip versions 22.3.1 and 23.3.2
1. pip-tools version: 7.4.1

#### Steps to replicate
I'm running pip-compile as part of a Bazel project to build my requirements lock file. Bazel does not install the libraries into the standard location or directory structure, so the caching mechanism doesn't quite work. I believe anyone who uses pip-compile without a corresponding pip install will hit this issue.

Consider the following requirements.in file, which contains only one dependency.

```
# requirements.in
torch==2.2.1+cu118
```

In a new Python virtual environment, run the following commands
```
pip install pip-tools
pip-compile --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118 --cache-dir SOME_CACHE_DIR --verbose
```

This downloads the pytorch library which is about 2 GB. Now run the command again.
```
pip-compile --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118 --cache-dir SOME_CACHE_DIR --verbose
```

The command seems to hang after the following output, but actually it is still running and resumes after around 30 seconds.
```
Using indexes:
  https://pypi.org/simple
  https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
  Looking in indexes: https://pypi.org/simple, https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118

                          ROUND 1
  Collecting torch==2.2.1+cu118
```

Here is what is happening during the second run.

1. Candidates for the package "torch" is sought from `SOME_CACHE_DIR/wheels/...` which fails because the wheel is not present. 
2. An HTTP request is created fetch the package again.
3. The cache controller reports an HTTP cache hit from `SOME_CACHE_DIR/http/...` because it was cached by the previous run of pip-compile.
4. The entire 2GB serialized response from the previous run is deserialized from disk so that its HTTP headers can be examined. (This takes 6 to 12 seconds on my machine.)
5. The cached response is determined to be stale because there is no "max-age" or "expires" header value. The response is tossed.
6. A conditional request is crafted, by adding the "If-None-Match" and "If-Modified-Since" headers. To set these values, the entire 2GB response is deserialized *again* from disk to retrieve the "Etag" and "Last-Modified" fields.
7. The request is sent and pytorch.org responds with 304 Not Modified.
8. The response is deserialized from disk *a third time* and the response body is written to disk in a new temporary directory `TMP_DIR/pip-unpack-xxxxx/torch-xxxxx.whl`.
9. The .whl file is read from disk so that hashes can be computed.
10. Regular behavior after this.

This ends up eating 2GB of disk space every time I run pip-compile by writing duplicate .whl files into the TMP_DIR. It also does not save time compared to actually downloading the .whl again because there are so many round trips to disk and time spent in messagepack serializing and deserializing the same file. I think the issue would be fixed if the .whl file is instead written to SOME_CACHE_DIR so that the caching mechanism could find it. Maybe this could be hacked in on the pip-tools side by copying and pasting any .whl files into SOME_CACHE_DIR. 



#### Expected result
Running pip-compile twice in a row with no requirements.in changes should be fast, and used cached .whl files from the first run.

#### Actual result
Running pip-compile twice in a row with no requirements.in changes is slow, and does not reuse .whl files from the first run directly. It instead recreates them from the http cache in a round-about way, and places the results in to TMP_DIR where they are not discovered by subsequent runs.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body: That's likely Pip's doing. When using package indexes with the metadata API, it's more efficient. Also, when the web server supports sending partial byte ranges, Pip's resolver can also only download the beginning of wheels that contain metadata. pip-tools doesn't handle caching by itself.

comments.author: axbycc-mark
comments.body: I have retested against pip 24.0 and the round-tripping issue was fixed. They separated out the header from the rest of the body so that the body is only loaded one time. However, the file copying issue persists. The .whl are copied to a TMP_DIR instead of the pip tool cache.

comments.author: axbycc-mark
comments.body:
> That's likely Pip's doing. When using package indexes with the metadata API, it's more efficient. Also, when the web server supports sending partial byte ranges, Pip's resolver can also only download the beginning of wheels that contain metadata. pip-tools doesn't handle caching by itself.

I figured. But I made the decision to post here because I thought maybe it's pip's expectation that dependency resolution would never occur without a corresponding install command. In that case, it would be pip-compile improperly calling down to pip. 

It could be pip-compile's responsibility to reach into the resolver.factory._link_candidate_cache to move all the files from the TMP_DIR into the pip-compile cache directory so that subsequent runs of pip-compile would find them.

Edit: I'm seeing after experimenting that pip does not automatically put installed .whl files into the cache directory like I thought. So the intended behavior from pip is to make a new copy of the pytorch whl into the temp directory every time you install it from cache.

issues.title: Add an option to track source file changes
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

I need a quick way to tell if requirements files need to be regenerated.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

The simplest solution is to keep a hash of the source file(s) in the header of the generated requirement files. That hash could be checked manually. This is particularly well-suited for individual requirements files.

For requirements from `pyproject.toml`, a better solution would be to generate a consistent hash of the extracted requirements, and have an option or command to only check if the generated source hash match with it's destination requirements. This method would allow unrelated `pyproject.toml` changes without having to regenerate the requirements and also work well with individual input files.

In our use case we commit the generated requirement files to allow predictable builds. This check could be used in PR or pre-merge tests to ensure no one has forgotten to regenerate the requirements. Users could also add a check to their own tools (eg pre-commit hook) to ensure they do not forget.

#### Alternative Solutions

The only alternative I can think of is to make a copy of the generated requirement files, update them then ensure they haven't been modified. This would be much slower.

#### Additional context

Other dependency tracking tools like Pipenv and, if I'm not mistaken, npm, also have a way to quickly detect discrepancies between the source and generated files.

If additional tampering protection is desired the hash could be generated from a combination of input and output (header with final hash excluded of course). This is not a requirement for me and although I have no issue with that per se, part of the reason I stopped using Pipenv was excessive tamper control: we had an issue (bug?) where it always updated unrelated deps and the way our internal index worked it often listed new versions that were not yet available, breaking the whole thing, and manual edits caused Pipenv to automatically regenerate it's lock file... but I'm disgressing, and it's not even something I ever had issue with using pip-tools (the update options / controls are perfect as far as I'm concerned).

I use pip-compile to hard-code the requirements for a release. I would like the build script to validate the requirements files so that the PR build fails if the requirements have not been updated after sources have been modified.

While this can be done by re-generating the dependencies, if the source file(s) for requirements are checksumed then it's also very quick and simple to tell if we might have to re-generate the deps and we can fail quickly.

Also with pip-compile it's easy to re-use the last release venv to speed things up, and if the generated requirements haven't changed that it will work without even needing PyPi. However, if I need to run pip-compile to make sure the requirement files aren't obsolete then I'll still need access to PyPi.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
> Is there an idea for how this will work? I'd expect to be able to move each `.in` template into a separate dependency group instead.

Yeah, that's kinda the use-case this PEP solves.

> Then `pip-compile pyproject.toml --group tests` would read the `tests` group from `pyproject.toml` and output to `tests.txt` (or to `-o {name}`). Does that sound reasonable?

This needs to be defined, I think. While working on support for the distribution package build dependencies (#1681 / https://pip-tools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/#maximizing-reproducibility), we realized that there would be cases where one would want to extract those dependencies in isolation and cases of getting combined deps (`--build-deps-for=wheel` / `--all-build-deps` / `--only-build-deps `).

There's a precedent that doing `pip-compile pyproject.toml requirements.in` works and sources the deps from several places. That can also be combined with `--extras`, IIRC.

So to proceed meaningfully, we need to define the semantics and UX for all of these combinations. Do we need `--[no-]runtime` or some other ways to distinguish what the users would like to encode in their constraint file generation requests? Additionally, I would like to keep #2124 in mind as well, while answering these questions.

> Currently I have different environments as separate templates: `requirements/test.in`, `requirements/typing.in`, etc. Now I'd have `tests` and `typing` dependency groups instead but otherwise get the same behavior.

Simlarly, I have even more envs defined, mostly one per tox target with multiple constraint files (aka DIY lock files) for each, since combinations of different platforms/runtimes can count as separate environments (fun stuff: https://github.com/ansible/awx-plugins/tree/c7fc0a1/dependencies/lock-files#readme).

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
Now that the `pip` implementation seems on track to merge and be part of `pip` 25.1 later this year, I'd like to start thinking about contributing a parallel feature here in `pip-tools` specifically for `pip-compile`.[^1]
I'd like to discuss the exact desired UX here, and hopefully I can work on a PR

[^1]: I'm assuming that the implementation will merge and release as-is. It's been approved but not yet merged, and nobody has raised objections to it in several weeks since the last changes.

The UX in `pip` is going to be `pip install --group test` as a shorthand for `pip install --group "./pyproject.toml:test"`.
You can specify `--group` multiple times and potentially use multiple distinct `pyproject.toml` files. e.g., It allows the following:
```
pip install \
    --group ./subproject1/pyproject.toml:typing \
    --group ./subproject2/pyproject.toml:typing
```

I'd like `pip-compile` to imitate this UX exactly, so that users have a consistent experience between tools.

What I'd implement would therefore be a `--group` option like `pip`'s, and the same deduplication/normalization pass over data using `dependency_groups`. We could either depend on `dependency_groups` directly or require `pip >= 25.1` (once available) and leverage the vendored copy from there. IMO either is fine, since `pip-tools` already reaches into `pip` internals.

I don't have any exciting releases planned for `dependency-groups`. Probably once `pip` supports `--group` I'll do a 2.0 release to remove the pip wrapper command. It depends only on `packaging`, nothing else.

Does this overall plan sound good? Does `pip-compile` want a different UX?

Okay. I don't like that it will drift from `pip` syntax but if it's consistent within `pip-tools` that might be best.

Just to lay out how it would look, here are the single vs double colon options, plus a third idea:

### Single Colon
- `pip install --group './foo/pyproject.toml:bar'`
- `pip-compile --group './foo/pyproject.toml:bar'`

### Double Colon
- `pip install --group './foo/pyproject.toml:bar'`
- `pip-compile --group './foo/pyproject.toml::bar'`

### 1-2 Colons

i.e. Make `::` and `:` both work as aliases/alternatives.

- `pip install --group './foo/pyproject.toml:bar'`
- `pip-compile --group './foo/pyproject.toml:bar'`
- `pip-compile --group './foo/pyproject.toml::bar'`

---

I'll work on an PR as soon as I'm able, using the double-colon syntax. If the 1-2 colon option looks nice, I'd be happy to pursue that as well.

comments.author: Gankra
comments.body:
Another update from `uv pip compile`:

We're planning to move forward with just support for `:` but if you ship `::` we'll add support both so that we're consistent with y'all and pip.

---
 
We're also planning to add subtle group context in `# via` comments (don't have our hearts set on the syntax here but that's what we have for now). So an invocation like this:

```
uv pip compile pyproject.toml --group subdir/pyproject.toml:foo
```
produces the following (note the `:foo` after `subdir/pyproject.toml`)

```
# This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
#    uv pip compile pyproject.toml --group subdir/pyproject.toml:foo
iniconfig==2.0.0
    # via mysubproject (subdir/pyproject.toml:foo)
typing-extensions==4.10.0
    # via myproject (pyproject.toml)
```

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
@Gankra to be in line with the build system extraction refs, the output would need to be
```diff
 # This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
 #    uv pip compile pyproject.toml --group subdir/pyproject.toml:foo
 iniconfig==2.0.0
-    # via mysubproject (subdir/pyproject.toml:foo)
+    # via mysubproject (subdir/pyproject.toml::dependency-groups.foo)

     # via myproject (pyproject.toml)
```

(see https://pip-tools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/#maximizing-reproducibility for the build deps refs output example that has things like `via my-cool-django-app (pyproject.toml::build-system.requires)`)

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
> Is there a particularly compelling reason not to support the upstream syntax here? (supporting two colons as well seems fine to me, but I don't have as much context as you)

So my reasoning was that (1) pip-tools doesn't really have an “upstream”. It happens to rely on parts of pip, but it performs semantically different tasks and the `pip-complile` CLI mostly doesn't seem to mimic pip, short of the `--pip-args` hack.
Another reason (2) is that we have `::` in the output.

In general, I don't think I'm strongly against a single colon. But then again, there are a few other patterns existing in the CLI that relate to extracting things out of `pyproject.toml` (like Poetry-specific sections, regular PEP 621, build deps) and they mostly allow a single `pyproject.toml`, not several IIRC, with various targets being requested via CLI options that don't include the file path.
I feel like following `pip` might cause UX confusion in this area. But at the same time, I don't have a better suggestion.

## Proposed Implementation Plan for PEP 735 Dependency Groups

I'd like to contribute an implementation for PEP 735 (dependency-groups) support in pip-tools.

### Scope
- Parse `[dependency-groups]` sections from `pyproject.toml`
- Add CLI flags: `--group <name>` / `--all-groups`
- Propagate group resolution to `pip compile` output
- Handle transitive dependencies within groups
- Add comprehensive tests matching existing test patterns

### Approach
1. Extend `pip_tools/resolver.py` to recognize dependency-groups
2. Update `pip_tools/cli.py` with new flags
3. Mirror the resolution logic already used for `--extra` and `--constraint`
4. Follow the existing test structure in `tests/`

### Timeline
- Week 1: Core parsing + resolution logic
- Week 2: CLI integration + edge case handling
- Week 3: Tests, docs, and review

Happy to discuss scope and adjust before starting. I've contributed to Python packaging tools before and am comfortable with the pip codebase.

Looking forward to contributing!

comments.author: hjoukl
comments.body:
Hi, for anyone stumbling over this:

I'm seeing the same issue, using 

```
pip-compile requirements.in --output-file requirements.txt --generate-hashes --no-emit-index-url --no-reuse-hashes --rebuild --upgrade-package pytaf --pre
```

This happens due to the package having changed in the package index, i.e. changed wheel contents and checksum, for the same name and version number.

While this is certainly not best practice we sometimes regenerate a package with modifications with the same version number, in this case in preparation for a prelease - and actually publish it (again) to an internal index.

As mentioned above `pip cache purge` doesn't fix the situation - because it's rather the pip-tools cache that is relevant here.

```
rm -fr ~/.cache/pip-tools/  # Linux
```

resolved it for me.

(you may or may not actually need to delete the pip cache too, but I can't test that right now - it's what I first tried so it's gone for now)

Cheers,
Holger

issues.title: [RFE] Output to `constraints.txt` by default
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Currently, `pip-compile` outputs to `requirements.txt` but I think that it's misleading as the output of the tool better maps to the concept of lockfiles (aka constraints in pip-speak).


#### Describe the solution you'd like

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->
I'd like pip-tools to be consistent with its own recommendations to use `pip install -c`.

#### Alternative Solutions

<!-- Have you tried to workaround the problem using pip-tools or other tools? Or a different approach to solving this issue? Please elaborate here. -->
..not doing so?

#### Additional context

<!-- Add any other context, links, etc. about the feature here. -->
Last year, I wrote this explanation about the misconceptions of pinning: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/1326#issuecomment-1834517252. And I figured that pip-tools itself is sending mixed messaging regarding what it does. I believe we can correct at least some of it.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
> I find it confusing that in some contexts "constraints" are required, while in others they are limits but not necessarily requirements. Usually I think of the term meaning the latter, as I don't know an alternative word for that.

@AndydeCleyre both requirements and constraints are pip-specific contexts. The latter is less known and is a set of additional restrictions that the dependency resolver applies only if it sees the listed projects during the process of resolution. Requirements, OTOH, are direct user requests to install something. So the difference is between "I want these installed" and "if these are going to end up selected for installations, here's the limits". I believe that pip-tools contributed to confusion by substituting the concepts in the readme/docs, combined with people not knowing at all that constraints are a thing. And that's my primary motivation — disentangling the concepts and educating the users. The filenames don't matter to pip — the contents just need to be text in the right format. Pip will work with `pip install -r constraints.txt` or `pip install pkg -c requirements.in` — these are confusing, should not be used with such names and cause cognitive dissonance, but they would work for as long as their contents look right to pip. Pip-tools (and dependabot) often advertises `requirements.in` and `requirements.txt`, while suggesting people to use the later as constaints as in `pip install -r requirements.in -c requirements.txt` — and I think this is the only right way to use these file pairs but I despise that the filenames create such confusion. I know that it's easy to detect such pairs for Dependabot which is why it's the only supported use in the context of that tool, but outside of it, I'd really like to push for naming things right and then integrating them correctly. Some time ago I produced this rant related to a series of misconceptions around constraints/lockfiles — https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/1326#issuecomment-1834517252 — and I think this misnaming is a contributing factor.

Technically, if organized right, sets/matrixes of constraint files are essentially a very much usable lockfile. In fact, that's how [rye](https://rye-up.com/) uses pip-tools today, per my understanding (I still haven't yet used rye myself, so this statement is probably a bit too simplistic).

So I want to reinforce the understanding that pip-tools' outputs are better treated as lockfiles while the inputs are for direct deps. Misusing constraints as requirements can lead to cases when the users are attempting to install things that are inherently incompatible with their environments, just because they were generated in (and for) other envs. But using them as constraints would not make pip error out if there's some entries that never hit the depresolver.

Also, some of the concerns around having dependencies that don't automatically pull in the package/wheel deps are going to be addressed by PEP 735 "Dependency Groups", I think.

3. A way to install what I need in dev: `pip install --find-links wheels -r src.in -r dev.in -c constraints.txt`
4. A way to install what I need in prod: `pip install --find-links wheels -r src.in -c constraints.txt`

comments.body:
The main thing I lose from something like this is a list of "these are the exact packages to install for src.in" in a static form. I'm losing that info and kicking it to `pip install` to redo all of the resolution and figure out that list. I have steps in my pipeline where I'd like to have that list so that I can pick out those libraries and build wheels for them similar to the `pip wheel` command above but working around limitations like that `pip wheel` doesn't build wheels in parallel.

An equivalent in another world is the `yarn.lock` which can be used to install everything, without the input `package.json`. This is similar to how pip-tools operates in the `-r` philosophy.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
> Just generate a monster constraints file of the entire possible dependency tree. Yes it might fail for some people and they can deal with platform-specific constraint files or have some options to ignore certain dependencies but gosh I'd love to have the option for a single cross-platform constraints file.

In #826, I realized that this is basically unrealistic with the current ecosystem. And it's because it's not always the right thing to do (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/1326#issuecomment-1834517252) but mostly about the impossibility to cross-compile (there's bits missing in CPython stdlib and other places in the ecosystem). For the time being, there is no way to compile sdists for some other environment. So no, it's not possible to just ignore env markers, it'd just explode during the dependency resolution, which is why I used GHA to generate an entire matrix of them (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/826#issuecomment-1324127670).

It's not about adding env markers into the constraint file, it's about being unable to resolve deps for trees involving platform-specific projects when there's sdists in the tree. FWIW pip-tools piggy-backs on pip's own depresolver, not adding much on top.

Besides, we probably shouldn't be reinventing the wheel while the effort to standardize the lockfiles is being debated on discuss.python.org as we speak (you should watch that discussion as it unfolds!).



> The main thing I lose from something like this is a list of "these are the exact packages to install for src.in" in a static form. I'm losing that info and kicking it to `pip install` to redo all of the resolution and figure out that list.

I don't think you lose the direct deps since they're listed in `.in` files that you pass via `-r`. And `pip show` will display if packages are deps of something else or pulled in directly. Also, passing `-c` lets pip's depresolver discard unusable options much faster, compared to installing without constraints and having to backtrack stuff.

> An equivalent in another world is the `yarn.lock` which can be used to install everything, without the input `package.json`. This is similar to how pip-tools operates in the `-r` philosophy.

Sounds like you want PEP 735 "dependency groups" here, rather than a distributable project deps. Except the yarn example corresponds to just one group of deps with no flexibility.

comments.author: webknjaz

issues.title: Get all build dependencies recusively?
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Hello. I want to be able to build all packages locally from source. To this end I need to download all runtime- and build time dependencies recursively. I thought that pip-tools would be able to compile a complete list of all dependencies, or at least several lists which complement each other.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

Here is a minimal example `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools", "setuptools-scm"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
requires-python = ">=3.9"
name = "foobar"
version = '0.0.1'
dependencies = ['django', 'twisted']
```

It depends on Django and [Twisted](https://twisted.org/). Twisted depends on [Constantly](https://github.com/twisted/constantly), which depends on [Versioneer](https://github.com/python-versioneer/python-versioneer) at build time (`versioneer[toml]==0.29` in `build-system.requires`). My understanding is that the following command should give me all build dependencies:

```sh
pip-compile --only-build-deps --all-build-deps pyproject.toml 
```

However, the output is missing Versioneer:

```
#
# This file is autogenerated by pip-compile with Python 3.12
# by the following command:
#
#    pip-compile --all-build-deps --only-build-deps pyproject.toml
#
packaging==23.2
    # via setuptools-scm
setuptools-scm==8.0.4
    # via foobar (pyproject.toml::build-system.requires)
typing-extensions==4.8.0
    # via setuptools-scm
wheel==0.41.3
    # via
    #   foobar (pyproject.toml::build-system.backend::editable)
    #   foobar (pyproject.toml::build-system.backend::wheel)

# The following packages are considered to be unsafe in a requirements file:
# setuptools
```

Maybe I am misunderstanding the purpose of `--all-build-deps`, or maybe there is something off with constantly?


#### Alternative Solutions

The only alternative I can think of is manually downloading all runtime- and build time dependencies, opening the tarballs, looking for a `pyproject.toml` in each one, looking for a `build-system.requires` entry and downloading those, then repeating the process until no new packages get downloaded.

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
At least at present, I don't think we can solve this. It would be interesting to pursue as a feature, but I worry it might be beyond what we can feasibly tackle.

`--all-build-deps` grabs build deps for all targets -- it is not inherently recursive, so the OP's behavior is as-expected.

Getting recursive build deps may actually require doing resolution, which can require _doing_ builds. I'm not closing as of yet, but I am considering whether or not this is a feature we really want to pursue.

issues.title: pip-compile should accept special files (pipes, fifo, pty, sockets, ...) as output files
issues.body:
When running `pip-compile -o /dev/stdout`, the command blocks indefinitely. It shouldn't and should write the requirement file in the given file, even if it's not a bare file. 

Please note that `pip-compile | <other program>` doesn't work either (the other program doesn't receive anything).

Please also note that `stderr` is cluttered by some eventual warnings not parseable by pip and is so not usable as a viable content source.

#### Environment Versions

1. > Linux VirtualBox 5.4.0-165-generic # 182-Ubuntu SMP Mon Oct 2 19:43:28 UTC 2023 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
1. > Python version: Python 3.8.10
1. > pip version: pip 23.3.1
1. > pip-tools version: pip-compile, version 7.3.0

#### Steps to replicate

1. `git clone <your favourite "using setup.py" project> && cd in`
2. `pip-compile setup.py -o /dev/stdout`
3. nothing happens

#### Expected result

output on stdout (**not stderr**)
warnings (if any) on stderr

#### Actual result
\<nothing and process blocked>


#### Steps to replicate (advanced)
TTY 1 :
1. `mkfifo /tmp/mylovelyfifo`
2. `cat /tmp/mylovelyfifo`

TTY 2 :
1. `git clone <your favourite "using setup.py" project> && cd in`
2. `pip-compile setup.py -o /tmp/mylovelyfifo`

#### Expected result

output on TTY 1
warnings (if any) on TTY 2

#### Actual result
\<nothing and process blocked>

comments.author: manuco
comments.body:
The main problem is that `pip compile` try to **read** the **output file** in order to find previous requirement and update it. `pip compile` should ensure that previous requirements is only read from a **real file** (with [stat.S_ISREG(mode)](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stat.html)), but should not trust that reading from this file won't block.

For example, setting `/dev/stdout` as an output file will make `pip compile` try to read this file. And it won't generate any error because `/dev/stdout` as a link to your terminal (`/dev/pts/*n*`) is also readable (since `/dev/pts/*n*` is also stdin and stderr). But it won't give any data until you type on your keyboard (which is not what's expected).

comments.body: Also the documentation should emphasize that `-` is a legit output filename redirecting it to `stdout`.

issues.title: support per-requirement options
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

`pip` supports [per-requirement options](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/requirements-file-format/#per-requirement-options), e.g. `--config-settings`

I'm forced to use per-requirement `--config-settings`, because there are [cases where pip intentionally does not honor the command-line `--config-settings`](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/build-system/pyproject-toml/#backend-configuration).

> Configuration settings provided via --config-settings command line options (or the equivalent environment variables or configuration file entries) are passed to the build of requirements explicitly provided as pip command line arguments. They are not passed to the build of dependencies, or to the build of requirements provided in requirement files.

But `pip-compile` does not seem to propagate per-requirement options.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like pip-compile to propagate per-requirement options from `.in` to `.txt`

```
$ echo 'scipy==1.10.1; --config-settings="setup-args=-Dblas=blas"' > r.in

$ pip-compile -r r.in
numpy==1.24.4
    # via scipy
scipy==1.10.1; --config-settings="setup-args=-Dblas=blas"
    # via -r r2.in
```

#### Alternative Solutions

Command line `pip --config-settings` doesn't work, because I'm passing a requirements file to `pip wheel`, and pip intentionally doesn't propagate the settings.

My current workaround is to build the affected packages separately, avoiding use of a requirements file.  But it's not good for my use case, which is to build all the transitive dependencies for an application (targeting an alternative python implementation).  `pip wheel -r ...` is best suited for this.

Mostly because I have it set up that way everywhere and it's easier for me to sync it across projects. Changes to the pattern usually cause a lot of burden to scale that across other places. But also being able to have it next to the other linters and have the results in pre-commit.ci.
Though, now that we have in-memory env generation fixed in tox API, I'd be curious to try writing a plugin that would ship a standard mypy invocation. Syncing something like `pip install tox-mypy` would definitely be easier.

comments.author: NYDJustin
comments.body:
Hi @sirosen, following up from the review discussion on #2490 — opening the tox question here as you suggested.

**Context:** #1928 asks for mypy coverage across pip versions. My #2490 attempt used a tox matrix (`py{39,314}-pip{lowest,latest}-mypy` envs). Your feedback: (1) pip versions shouldn't be repeated in fresh tox envs — they should be shareable, and (2) the `getattr()`/`setattr()` version-compat approach is a short-term hack.

**Questions before I rework anything:**
1. Would a tox-based mypy matrix be acceptable in principle if the envs reference shared pip-version lists instead of repeating versions per env?
2. For version-conditional attribute access under mypy: pip's private APIs genuinely differ across 22.2 → 26.x, and the `pip._internal` stubs give no version-conditional way to express that. Is there a shape you'd accept — e.g. a small typed compat shim with explicit version guards — or would you rather mypy stay pinned to a single pip version?

Happy to go whichever direction you prefer — just didn't want to build the wrong thing twice.

issues.title: pre-commit hook for pip-sync
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

With the pre-commit hook for pip-compile (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/974), I am confident that any changes that I do in my development environment will be pinned. I would like to have the same for pip-sync so that nobody's development environment gets outdated.

In a project, it might be that one of the collaborators have modified the dependencies and pushed their new pip-compiled requirements.txt. As I get their changes via a `git pull`, I want to be sure that we (everyone) keep sharing the same dependencies. As far as I see with the current pip-tools workflow, pip-sync has to be run manually. That means, I have to be informed by the collaborator or check the pulled/merged commits to see if I need to run pip-sync. This could lead to some issues, could we automate pip-sync so that we avoid those?

If it gets implemented, the new hook combined with the existing pip-compile hook would allow a mostly automated dependency management.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I am no expert at pre-commit, but I think it can be used for developing a new hook similar to that of pip-compile(https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/pull/976). I believe one can use the [post-merge](https://pre-commit.com/#post-merge) `stage` for this hook.

.pre-commit-hooks.yaml for the new hook would something like the following:

```yaml
- id: pip-sync
  name: pip-sync
  description: Automatically sync requirements.
  entry: pip-sync
  language: python
  files: ^requirements\.(in|txt)$
  args: [--ask]
  
```

#### Alternative Solutions

Simply printing a message that the environment needs to modified could be a better default option as it is not intrusive (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/1076). The default hook configuration can use `--dry-run` for the args. Users who want automation can change in their .pre-commit-config.yaml by modifying the args from `--dry-run` to `--ask` instead.

For the dependencies which are using semantic versioning, it would ideally automatically sync changes in the minor and patch version and ask only for major version changes.

I am new to pip-tools and perhaps I am missing a point. If so, please share your existing solutions/workflows.

#### Additional context

https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks#_post_merge

Thank you for pip-tools.

issues.title: When having circular depenedcies in packages, the package is added in old and released version
issues.body:
<!-- Describe the issue briefly here. -->

In [napari](https://github.com/napari/napari) project, we are using `pip-compile` to [pin dependencies](https://github.com/napari/napari/tree/main/resources/constraints) for testing (to reduce test failures not related to PR). 

We are currently working on extracting part of the project to sub-packages. But if the subpackage requires some utils that are not yet extracted from the base package then `pip-compile` results in adding the package itself to dependencies. 

So it ends in having `napari (setup.cfg)` and `napari` in the comments of constraints, but also pin the release version of the project. 

I know that the best solution is to extract the code required by `napari` and `napari-plugin-manager` to the third package, but it could be the long-term target.

I think that do not notice that `napari` package is already defined as a project that is compiled using `pip-compile` is a bug and `napari==0.4.15` should not be put in output.

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Linux 
1. Python version: `$ 3.8 - 3.11
1. pip version: 23.1.2
1. pip-tools version: 6.13.0

issues.title: Upgrading an extra package leaks it into the install_requires
issues.body:
I think I've hit an edge case with pip-tools and setuptools. I couldn't find a similar open issue.

When selectively upgrading packages for the base dependencies (`install_requires`), requesting an upgrade for a package that's declared in the optional dependencies (`extras_require`) causes it to leak into the generated `requirements.txt` file, **even if the `--extra` was *not* selected**.

#### Environment Versions

1. Pop!_OS 22.04 LTS
1. Python 3.11.3
1. pip 23.1.2
1. pip-compile, version 6.13.0

#### Steps to replicate

1. create `setup.py`
```
echo 'from setuptools import setup

setup(
    install_requires=["requests"],
    extras_require={"dev": ["hodor"]},
)' > setup.py
```

2. prepare environment
```
virtualenv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install pip-tools
# generate initial requirements.txt
.venv/bin/pip-compile --resolver backtracking
```

3. upgrade an optional dependency and a dependency that's not declared anywhere
```
.venv/bin/pip-compile --resolver backtracking -P hodor -P numpy -o broken-requirements.txt
```

#### Expected result

```
certifi==2023.5.7
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.1.0
    # via requests
idna==3.4
    # via requests
requests==2.31.0
    # via UNKNOWN (setup.py)
urllib3==2.0.2
    # via requests
```

#### Actual result

```
certifi==2023.5.7
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.1.0
    # via requests
hodor==1!0  #  <------------------- shouldn't be here
idna==3.4
    # via requests
requests==2.31.0
    # via UNKNOWN (setup.py)
urllib3==2.0.2
    # via requests
```

pip-tools correctly ignores the `numpy` package, as it is not declared anywhere, but seems to be tricked by `hodor`, which is an extra dependency from the `dev` group. It is also missing the comment that tells why the dependency was included.

I've checked with a plain setup.py and a combination of setup.py and setup.cfg and both trigger this behavior.  Does not seem related to the choice of resolver either. Using a `requirements-dev.in` that references a `requirements.in` seems to work as expected.

comments.author: atugushev
comments.body:
Hey @giovannipcarvalho,

Thanks for the issue! Nice catch and great analysis.

comments.author: raabf
comments.body:
The same issue applies for `pyproject.toml` with its `[project.optional-dependencies]` extras section.

I currently workaround this issue by running a wrapper script which creates a temporary copy of `setup.cfg` where the `[options.extras_require]` section is removed, and after `pip-compile` restore the original `setup.cfg`.

issues.title: Request: making `--no-emit-index-url` the default of `pip-compile`
issues.body:
<!-- Describe the issue briefly here. -->

### Motivation

Currently, `pip-compile` by default will emit any index URLs used.

For open source users, likely this will be empty (no index URL).  Regardless of the default being `--no-emit-index-url` or not, these users will not be affected, as just PyPI is used.

For non-open source users, this may not be empty.  For these users, forgetting to include `--no-emit-index-url` represents a security risk, because if this opt-in arg is forgotten, a company secret will be leaked.

This actually happened to me tonight when I accidentally leaked my company's internal package manager's index URL.  Luckily, I realized it within 15 minutes, and refreshed my token.  Now I am getting an email from GitGuardian saying their service detected a string secret was leaked.

For all of my company's `pip-compile` use cases, we append `--no-emit-index-url`.  Thus for engineers at my company, a useful default would be `--no-emit-index-url`.

### Request

I think the default of `pip-compile` should be secure (and not bias towards leaking secrets).

This entails:
1. Making `--no-emit-index-url` the new default
2. Adding `--emit-index-url` or `--enable-emit-index-url` as an opt-in flag

EDIT:

Understood. Thanks for reporting, sounds like a reasonable request!

Yeah sorry for being unclear there, I just meant open source users likely don't use package mangers beside PyPI, so they don't have an extra index URL.

Here is a slightly more backwards compatible idea:
1. `pip-compile` continues with the current default of emitting index URLs
2. Enable `pip-compile` to detect if a secret is present inside an extra index URL
3. Unless a flag `--allow-secrets-in-index-url` is passed, `pip-compile` will throw a nonzero exit code

That way, users who don't have secrets in the index URL can still rely on index URL being emitted by default.

issues.title: pip-compile with --index-url fails to handle sdists
issues.body:
I'm trying to use pip-tools in an environment where we have access to a caching proxy (Artifactory) of pypi.org but no direct access to pypi.org.

In most situations, I'm able to run `pip-compile` in a virtualenv where I've set `index-url` in `pip.conf`, and everything works. However, I'm now trying to get dependabot working, and dependabot invokes `pip-compile` and passes `--index-url`, but doesn't set `index-url` for `pip` in any way (environment variables or `pip.conf`). 

In this environment (and in my local environment I can reproduce it, if I move `pip.conf` aside), when `pip-compile` encounters a package that only has an sdist and not a wheel (e.g. defopt), it tries to run `python setup.py egg_info` on the sdist, and that runs `python3 -m pip --disable-pip-version-check wheel --no-deps -w /tmp/something --quiet setuptools_scm>=3.3`, which fails after trying to connect to `pypi.org` and getting blocked at our firewall.

I think, probably, `pip-compile --index-url` should change how it invokes `python setup.py egg_info` such that that call is also aware of the index url. One simple way would be to set `PIP_INDEX_URL`, but you all probably could get more clever about pip than I can.

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Linux (Debian 10)
1. Python version: `$ python -V` 3.11.1
1. pip version: `$ pip --version` 23.0.1
1. pip-tools version: `$ pip-compile --version` 6.12.3

#### Steps to replicate

1. Create a `requirements.in` containing one line, `defopt`
2. Block access to pypi.org, use some alternative pypi mirror (devpi would be fine)
3. Run `pip-compile -vv --index-url=https://pypi.internal/simple --resolver backtracking requirements.in`

#### Expected result

It should result in a `requirements.txt` file.

#### Actual result

The command fails, with some stacktraces ending in `pip._internal.exceptions.MetadataGenerationFailed: metadata generation failed`

issues.title: Error: input and output filenames must not be matched
issues.body:
Error: input and output filenames must not be matched

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Windows 11
2. Python version: 3.9.17
3. pip version: 23.0.1
4. pip-tools version: 6.12.2

#### Steps to replicate

Using command as per comments in and existing compiled requirements.txt after adding a new dependency in file.

```
#
# This file is autogenerated by pip-compile with Python 3.9
# by the following command:
#
#    pip-compile --annotation-style=line ./bin/app/requirements.txt
#
click==8.1.3              # via flask
flask==2.2.2              # via flask-failsafe
flask-failsafe==0.2       # via -r ./bin/app/requirements.txt
importlib-metadata==6.0.0  # via flask
itsdangerous==2.1.2       # via flask
jinja2==3.1.2             # via flask
markupsafe==2.1.2         # via jinja2, werkzeug
werkzeug==2.2.2           # via flask
zipp==3.11.0              # via importlib-metadata
gunicorn # New dependecy
```

Executed

`pip-compile --annotation-style=line ./bin/app/requirements.txt`

#### Expected result

File recompiled with new dependency fixed and added dependencies.

#### Actual result

`Error: input and output filenames must not be matched`

#### Notes

This appears to be caused by changes in this PR https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/pull/1787 "Raise error if input and output filenames are matched"

I can understand thinking behind the change but there is little risk of updating file in place when using version control, it means that to add a new dependency I have to copy the file first and add an --output-file parameter, then delete the input file, or manage two files in the repository going forward.

It is also at odds with the deriving of output file name from input as specified as a option in help:

```
  -o, --output-file FILENAME      Output file name. Required if more than one
                                  input file is given. Will be derived from
                                  input file otherwise.
```

It breaks backwards compatibility withe the command list in comments in the output file.

Suggestion either remove this check or add a flag such as `--allow-overwrite` to suppress the check.

comments.author: AndydeCleyre
comments.body:
The idea of the tool is to keep a `requirements.in` file with your explicit, top level dependencies, versioned as loosely as possible, then generate a fully version locked, deep dependency tree/list as `requirements.txt`.

If you then remove the `.in` file and compile using the locked `.txt` as a source, you lose the information of which dependencies are explicit/top level, and you lose the possibility of the versions getting updated, because they're already locked in exactly.

It is very unlikely that is any user's intent.

comments.author: PaulBurridge
comments.body:
It is not necessary to use a separate file to tell the top level dependencies as below: 

`# via -r requirements.txt` - top level
`# via -r requirements.txt, flask` - dependency of flask

We have many developers who are not used to using pip-compile who simply seek out a `requirements.txt` file to add dependencies to, we would prefer this continued to be possible going forward. 

The tool has worked fine using a single file before this change and if the "idea of this tool" is not to ever use a single file why does the help for `--output-file` specify `Required if more than one input file is given.  Will be derived from input file otherwise`?

comments.author: PaulBurridge
comments.body: Also to update versions we simply delete those that are not top level from the file, remove any relevant fixed version then recompile.

The way you're doing it, if an item is both a top level requirement and required by another package, you will have to remember that fact, it won't be reflected in your output.

> ... if the "idea of this tool" is not to ever use a single file why does the help for `--output-file` specify `Required if more than one input file is given.  Will be derived from input file otherwise`?

That's two files, not a single file. The input file is the `.in`, and the output file is the `.txt`.

comments.author: AndydeCleyre
comments.body: If you need to specify a version range, that will also be lost during compilation, and you'll need to remember that too.

comments.author: PaulBurridge
comments.body:
I have always run without specifying an output file and before the change it did overwrite the existing file which suggests that is a valid workflow by design. (see below)

```
#
# This file is autogenerated by pip-compile with Python 3.9
# by the following command:
#
#    pip-compile --annotation-style=line ./bin/app/requirements.txt
#
```

comments.author: acdha
comments.body: I think the logic on this change is reasonable but it could be better communicated since it was a breaking change in a minor point release and the message "Raise error if input and output filenames are matched" doesn't communicate the actual problem and the behaviour now conflicts with documentation for the `-O` option. If the error message said something like "The input name should not be the same as the output name" (ideally with either more documentation or a link to explain the philosophy) it would be easier to understand why this behaviour is desirable rather than the bug it appears to be when you first encounter it.

issues.title: Unable to upgrade a tightly-coupled dependency
issues.body:
My project depends on two packages, `dagster` and `dagster-k8s` (and actually many more, including more `dagster-*` packages - but let's stick to two for this explanation).

Dagster uses a tightly-coupled versioning scheme. The dagster libraries (like `dagster-k8s`) are always pinned to exact versions of the dagster core library (`dagster`).  So, for example:
 - `dagster-k8s 0.17.19` requires `dagster==1.1.19`
 - `dagster-k8s 0.17.20` requires `dagster==1.1.20`
 - `dagster-k8s 0.17.21` requires `dagster==1.1.21`
And so on. Each `dagster` release is accompanied by a release of all these library packages with a matching version.

I'd like to constrain the version of `dagster` that I use, and have `pip-compile` compute the appropriate version of all dagster libraries. This seems to work exactly once. After applying the constraint the first time, I can't upgrade.

I have a `setup.cfg` that includes
```cfg
[options]
install_requires =
    dagster>=1.1.20
    dagster-k8s
```

I pip-compiled this a while ago, and it all worked. Dependencies are all resolved.

Now I want to upgrade to the latest dagster-core, `dagster 1.1.21`. I update my setup.cfg:

```cfg
[options]
install_requires =
    dagster>=1.1.21
    dagster-k8s
```

I try to `pip-compile -P dagster`, but no dice, because the previous `pip-compile` step pinned `dagster` through the `dagster-k8s` dependency:

```
There are incompatible versions in the resolved dependencies:
  dagster==1.1.21 (from pip-tools-bug-demo-spenczar (pyproject.toml))
  dagster==1.1.20 (from dagster-k8s==0.17.20->pip-tools-bug-demo-spenczar (pyproject.toml))
```

I try it with the backtracking resolver, and get an analagous error:
```
pip._vendor.resolvelib.resolvers.ResolutionImpossible: [RequirementInformation(requirement=SpecifierRequirement('dagster==1.1.21'), parent=None), RequirementInformation(requirement=SpecifierRequirement('dagster==1.1.20'), parent=LinkCandidate('https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/bb/02/6ff11cae47979838b5b7f7e8731c4bac4ad984be4b86fef99ddcfe257608/dagster_k8s-0.17.20-py3-none-any.whl (from https://pypi.org/simple/dagster-k8s/)'))]
```

I still get the same errors if I try `pip-compile --upgrade-package dagster`.

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: MacOS
1. Python version: Python 3.9.6 and Python 3.10.10, at least.
1. pip version: pip 23.0.1
1. pip-tools version: pip-compile, version 6.12.2

#### Steps to replicate

1. Make a barebones project
```sh
mkdir pip-tools-bug-demo
cd pip-tools-bug-demo
echo "[options]
install_requires =
    dagster==1.1.20
    dagster-k8s
" > setup.cfg
```
3. Run pip-compile
```sh
pip-compile --resolver=backtracking
```
4. Change the version constraint to upgrade dagster
```sh
echo "[options]
install_requires =
    dagster==1.1.21
    dagster-k8s
" > setup.cfg
```
5. Try to pip-compile again to upgrade
```sh
pip-compile --resolver=backtracking
```

#### Expected result

I expect a `requirements.txt` to be written with `dagster==1.1.21` and `dagster-k8s==0.17.21` specified.

#### Actual result

This is presented as unresolveable (which is not really true):
```
  ERROR: Cannot install UNKNOWN (pyproject.toml) and dagster==1.1.21 because these package versions have conflicting dependencies.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/swnelson/.pyenv/versions/3.10.10/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pip/_internal/resolution/resolvelib/resolver.py", line 92, in resolve
    result = self._result = resolver.resolve(
  File "/Users/swnelson/.pyenv/versions/3.10.10/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pip/_vendor/resolvelib/resolvers.py", line 481, in resolve
    state = resolution.resolve(requirements, max_rounds=max_rounds)
  File "/Users/swnelson/.pyenv/versions/3.10.10/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pip/_vendor/resolvelib/resolvers.py", line 385, in resolve
    raise ResolutionImpossible(self.state.backtrack_causes)
pip._vendor.resolvelib.resolvers.ResolutionImpossible: [RequirementInformation(requirement=SpecifierRequirement('dagster==1.1.21'), parent=None), RequirementInformation(requirement=SpecifierRequirement('dagster==1.1.20'), parent=LinkCandidate('https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/bb/02/6ff11cae47979838b5b7f7e8731c4bac4ad984be4b86fef99ddcfe257608/dagster_k8s-0.17.20-py3-none-any.whl (from https://pypi.org/simple/dagster-k8s/)'))]
```
